analysis.one_liner: Preempts state product liability law to limit lawsuits against product manufacturers.
analysis.headline: The product liability overhaul gained 162 cosponsors but never got a committee or floor vote and died when the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: H.R. 3030, the Fairness in Product Liability Act of 1991, would have replaced state product liability law with a federal standard for lawsuits against companies whose products injure people. It would have shortened the time to sue to two years, restricted punitive damages, forced workers' compensation awards to be subtracted from jury awards, and barred most lawsuits against manufacturers once workers' compensation had paid [S2][S3]. The bill was introduced on July 25, 1991, referred to the Energy and Commerce and Judiciary Committees, and then sent to a subcommittee on August 30, 1991. It never received a committee vote or a floor vote and died when the Congress ended on January 3, 1993 [S1][S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Manufacturers and sellers of consumer products — including drug and medical-supply makers — and their liability insurers would have gained if the bill had passed. It would have set one federal standard superseding state laws, capped punitive damages, cut the filing window to two years, and shielded manufacturers from most suits once workers' compensation had paid an injured worker [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: The bill would supersede State law and set one federal standard governing product liability actions brought in either State or Federal court against a manufacturer or product seller [S2].
It would require product liability actions to be brought within two years after the harm and its cause is, or with reasonable diligence should have been, discovered [S2].
Compliance with knowledge common to the class of persons who used the product would not by itself give rise to punitive damages, limiting a category of large jury awards [S3].

Workers' compensation benefits already paid would be subtracted from a product liability award, and suits could be stayed until the full workers' compensation amount is determined; once workers' compensation paid, most other claims against the manufacturer would be barred [S3].

analysis.who_pays: People injured by defective products would bear the cost if it had become law: a shorter two-year filing window, limits on punitive damages, deductions of workers' compensation from awards, and preemption of stronger state consumer-protection and liability rules [S2][S3]. States would lose their authority over these cases [S2].

drawbacks.text: Opponents of bills like this argue the two-year discovery deadline and punitive-damage limits would leave people seriously injured by defective drugs, medical supplies, or other products without full compensation, and federal preemption would override stronger state consumer protections [S2][S3].

Supporters would argue manufacturers faced unpredictable, varying state liability rules and that limits on awards and uniform federal standards would reduce litigation costs passed into product prices; the bill's title itself framed the change as fairness to defendants [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Had it passed, the bill would have traded uniformity and lower litigation risk for manufacturers against weaker compensation for injured people and the loss of state-level protections. Because it never reached a vote, no such trade took place and existing state law remained in force [S2][S5].

outcome.mechanism: Referred to two committees the day it was introduced and to a subcommittee five weeks later, it never got a committee vote or a floor vote before the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993.

narrative.text: H.R. 3030 was introduced in the House on July 25, 1991, and referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce and the House Committee on Judiciary [S5].
On August 30, 1991, it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Commerce, Consumer Protection and Competitiveness, where it stayed [S5].
No markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever occurred; the bill died when the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: People injured by defective products kept their existing state-law rights to sue, including longer filing windows and punitive damages; manufacturers and insurers never got the federal shield. The cosponsors' bill went nowhere.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Injured consumers, whose lawsuit rights were preserved

sides.party_line_note: The 162 cosponsors split 112 Republicans and 50 Democrats, with a Democratic sponsor, but the record shows no vote or recorded opposition — the bill simply never left committee [S4][S5].

industries.industry: Product manufacturers (including drug and medical-supply makers)
industries.note: Had it passed, the bill would have preempted state liability rules, limited punitive damages, shortened the filing window to two years, and barred most suits once workers' compensation paid — the subjects listed include drugs, medical supplies, and product safety [S2][S3]. Its interest runs against people seeking compensation for defective products.
Caps on punitive damages, shorter filing windows, and a single federal standard would have reduced insurers' exposure on product liability claims.
The bill would have cut the number and size of consumer product liability suits, the core business of lawyers who represent injured plaintiffs.
